principle.name: Think Full-Stack, Not Just Layers
principle.description: Always consider the entire technology stack when making decisions. Every layer impacts others - database design affects API contracts, frontend state management affects backend services, and deployment affects everything.
principle.rationale: Full-stack development requires holistic thinking to avoid creating siloed solutions that don't integrate well.

example.scenario: When designing a user authentication system
example.good: Consider how JWT tokens will be stored, validated, and refreshed across frontend and backend
example.bad: Designing authentication only for the API without considering frontend token management

principle.name: Integration First, Implementation Second
principle.description: Prioritize getting the full system working with basic functionality before adding features or optimizations.
principle.rationale: It's better to have a complete, working system than a partially implemented complex one.

example.good: Implement basic CRUD operations first, then add advanced features like real-time updates
example.bad: Trying to implement everything at once without testing basic functionality

principle.name: Type Safety Across the Stack
principle.description: Ensure type safety from database to frontend to prevent runtime errors and improve developer experience.
principle.rationale: TypeScript provides compile-time checking; shared types prevent mismatches between API contracts and frontend usage.

example.good: Use shared TypeScript interfaces for API responses and frontend props
example.bad: Duplicating type definitions or using 'any' types throughout the stack

principle.name: Security by Design, Not as Afterthought
principle.description: Build security considerations into every layer from the beginning, not as an add-on.
principle.rationale: Security is much harder and more expensive to retrofit than to build in from the start.

example.good: Use established security patterns like password hashing, JWT with proper expiration, and role-based access control
example.bad: Storing passwords in plain text, using session IDs without validation, or implementing custom crypto without security review

principle.name: Performance Everywhere
principle.description: Consider performance implications at every layer - database queries, API response times, frontend rendering, and network requests.
principle.rationale: Performance issues in one layer often cascade to affect the entire user experience.

example.good: Use efficient WebSocket connections, implement proper connection pooling, and consider bandwidth limitations
example.bad: Creating new WebSocket connections for every message without connection management or ignoring mobile network constraints

convention.rule: Use consistent naming conventions across the stack

template.pre: apps/ ├── user-application/ # Frontend ├── src/ │ ├── components/ # Reusable UI components │ ├── pages/ # Route components │ ├── hooks/ # Custom hooks │ ├── lib/ # Shared utilities │ └── types/ # Shared TypeScript types └── api/ # Backend API routes ├── src/ │ ├── controllers/ # API controllers │ ├── services/ # Business logic │ ├── models/ # Data models │ ├── middleware/ # Express middleware │ └── utils/ # Backend utilities └── database/ # Database schemas and migrations └── shared/ # Shared types and utilities

convention.rule: Design APIs with frontend consumption in mind

examples.good: Include pagination, filtering, and sorting parameters in API responses
Return consistent error response format with proper HTTP status codes
examples.bad: Returning unpaginated data sets without metadata or using inconsistent error formats

convention.rule: Test at every layer with appropriate tools

examples.good: Unit tests for business logic, integration tests for APIs, and E2E tests for user workflows
examples.bad: Only testing the UI without backend integration or testing APIs with mock data that doesn't match real scenarios

pitfall.why_problematic: Leads to data inconsistencies, duplicated logic, and poor user experience when frontend and backend get out of sync.
pitfall.correct_approach: Always define clear contracts between layers and use shared types to ensure consistency.

pitfall.why_problematic: Adding complex abstractions, microservices, or advanced patterns before the basic functionality is working leads to longer development time and harder maintenance.
pitfall.correct_approach: Start simple and add complexity only when the need is clearly demonstrated. Follow the YAGNI principle - You Aren't Gonna Need It Yet.

pitfall.why_problematic: Security vulnerabilities in full-stack applications can be catastrophic, affecting all layers and user data.
pitfall.correct_approach: Implement security best practices from day one, use established libraries for authentication and authorization, and never store sensitive data improperly.

pitfall.why_problematic: Inconsistent error handling makes debugging difficult and provides poor user experience.
pitfall.correct_approach: Implement centralized error handling, use structured logging, and provide meaningful error messages to users while logging detailed technical information for debugging.

category.name: architecture_design
category.item: Database schema supports all required API operations
API contracts are shared between frontend and backend
Authentication flow works seamlessly across all layers
Real-time features are properly architected for scalability
State management strategy is appropriate for application complexity
Error handling is comprehensive and user-friendly

category.name: implementation_quality
category.item: Code follows established patterns and conventions
All layers are properly tested (unit, integration, E2E)
Performance requirements are met (response times, memory usage)
Security best practices are implemented throughout the stack
